title: Arjuna forgets the Gita
hook: after the war, in a quiet palace hall, Arjuna admits to Krishna that he has forgotten the teaching he heard on the battlefield
carry: svadhyaya: return to the teaching every day

segments.voice: Yesterday Ashvamedhika opened with Yudhishthira on the riverbank and Vyasa pointing to old King Marutta's gold. Your line was mourning has its days; then dharma calls you up.

I've forgotten it. That, in plain terms, is what Arjuna tells Krishna. The war is over. The two friends are walking in the great assembly hall the Pandavas have won back, with time on their hands at last. And Arjuna brings up the conversation in the chariot, between the two armies, before the fighting began: the teaching people now call the Bhagavad Gita. What you told me then, he says, has slipped from my mind. Please tell it to me again.
screen: `THE WAR IS OVER.` → `A WALK IN THE HALL.` → `"I'VE FORGOTTEN IT."`

segments.voice: Krishna doesn't pretend that's fine. In Ganguli's telling he's displeased. You didn't hold on to what I told you in confidence, he says, and I'm sorry you forgot it. Then something surprising: he can't simply repeat it. He spoke on the battlefield, he explains, while united in yoga, and he can't call it back word for word. So instead he tells Arjuna an old story. A brahmana meets a perfected sage, a siddha, and asks the big questions: how a living being dies, how it is born again, what binds it to action, and how it goes free. More old dialogues follow. Together these chapters are known as the Anugita. They return to the Gita's ground, the self, action and freedom, but in a new shape: no army, no chariot, just questions asked in peace. Even Arjuna, who heard the Gita face to face, lost hold of it once the crisis passed. Insight doesn't keep by itself. This is why Hindus don't read the Gita once and shelve it. The practice is called svadhyaya, one's own study: coming back to sacred words again and again. Many families read a chapter a day; some learn a verse a week; some gather to chant the whole Gita on Gita Jayanti. Not because they've never heard it. Because, like Arjuna, they know it slips. Krishna doesn't hand Arjuna the old words. He sits down in the hall and starts again.
screen: `KRISHNA IS DISPLEASED` · `"I SPOKE IT IN YOGA"` · `THE ANUGITA: THE TEACHING RETOLD` · then, large: `SVADHYAYA: COME BACK TO IT AGAIN`

segments.voice: If you have a Gita or another sacred book at home, open it anywhere and read one verse slowly, twice. If not, bring back one line from these lessons. Breathe in the line; breathe out and say it to yourself in your own words, as if for the first time. If you pray, offer it back; if you don't, simply keep it with you for the day.
Ashvamedhika. The book where Arjuna admits he has forgotten, and Krishna teaches again, in a new shape.
Your line: svadhyaya, return to the teaching every day. Even Arjuna had to ask a second time. Day eight hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: The Anugita is read by students of the Mahabharata alongside the Bhagavad Gita, and commentators and teachers in several Hindu traditions have discussed how the two teachings relate.

Anugita.meaning: the 'after-Gita': Krishna's later teaching, told through old dialogues

brahmana.meaning: a member of the priestly and learned class

yoga.meaning: union; here, Krishna's deep inner absorption

notes: All paraphrase. The hook's "I've forgotten it" is a plain-English gloss of Arjuna's request, set in quotation marks as speech, not a quotation of Ganguli.
Confirm in Ganguli: Krishna's displeasure, his statement that he cannot repeat the teaching in full because it was spoken while he was in yoga, and the setting in the assembly hall.
The order and naming of the Anugita's embedded dialogues (brahmana and siddha, brahmana and wife, preceptor and disciple) should be checked against Ganguli's section headings.
No claim is made about the date or authorship relation between the Anugita and the Bhagavad Gita.
